clinicalPearls: A rare, benign condition of young women and adolescents in which one ovary becomes markedly enlarged by stromal oedema
It is thought to result from partial or intermittent torsion around the mesovarium that obstructs venous and lymphatic drainage while sparing arterial inflow
Presentation is with pelvic or abdominal pain and a palpable mass, closely mimicking ovarian torsion or a neoplasm
Imaging shows a diffusely enlarged, oedematous ovary, often with follicles displaced to the periphery and central stromal oedema
Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrates a strikingly oedematous stroma that is high in signal on T2-weighted sequences
Tumour markers are usually normal, which helps to distinguish it from a true ovarian neoplasm
Fertility-sparing surgery, such as detorsion with ovarian fixation, is preferred over oophorectomy in these young patients
reference.pathophysiology: Partial or intermittent torsion of the ovary about its vascular pedicle in the mesovarium obstructs the lower-pressure venous and lymphatic outflow while the arterial supply continues to fill the organ. Fluid therefore accumulates within the ovarian stroma, producing progressive, sometimes massive, oedematous enlargement of the ovary. The resulting mass can closely resemble a neoplasm both clinically and radiologically, yet the underlying process is benign and potentially reversible if recognised and treated conservatively.
additionalDifferentials: Ovarian neoplasm such as a fibroma
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal or transabdominal ultrasound with Doppler showing an enlarged ovary with peripheral follicles
Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrating stromal oedema with high T2 signal
Tumour markers, which are typically normal and help exclude malignancy
Assessment of arterial and venous flow to evaluate the degree of torsion
Histological examination if the ovary is removed, confirming stromal oedema without neoplasia
redFlags: Complete torsion with compromised ovarian viability
Inability to exclude malignancy, risking unnecessary oophorectomy
Acute severe pain with signs of an ischaemic ovary
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign with a good prognosis; ovary-sparing surgery preserves ovarian function and fertility, and outcomes are excellent when the diagnosis is recognised before radical surgery is undertaken.
pitfalls: Performing an unnecessary oophorectomy in a young woman by mistaking oedema for a tumour
Failing to consider fertility preservation when planning surgery
Overlooking intermittent torsion as the underlying mechanism
Not recognising the characteristic imaging appearance of stromal oedema
management: Ovary-sparing surgery (detorsion with wedge resection or biopsy) to preserve ovarian function and fertility, avoiding unnecessary oophorectomy
Intra-operative frozen-section histology to confirm the benign oedematous process and exclude neoplasm before deciding the extent of surgery
Oophoropexy (fixation) to reduce the risk of recurrent torsion, given intermittent torsion as the underlying mechanism
Analgesia and supportive care for the acute pelvic pain
Postoperative imaging follow-up to confirm resolution and monitor ovarian recovery
Refer to gynaecology, with fertility-preservation counselling in young women and adolescents
